CSVHandler

class CSVHandler(dialect='custom_ttea', delimiter=';', quotechar='"', doublequote=True, skipinitialspace=True, lineterminator='\n', quoting=0)[source]

Bases: object

Read and write CSV files with a custom dialect.

Fully integrated with the application’s singleton logger. Works with file paths or already-opened file-like objects (e.g. locked via portalocker). Handles common real-world issues: file locked by Excel, wrong encoding, corrupted files, missing directories, permission errors, etc.

Parameters:
dialectstr, optional

Name of the CSV dialect to register and use. Default is "custom_ttea".

delimiterstr, optional

Field delimiter character. Default is ";".

quotecharstr, optional

Character used to quote fields containing special characters. Default is '"'.

doublequotebool, optional

Whether a quotechar inside a field is doubled. Default is True.

skipinitialspacebool, optional

When True, whitespace immediately following the delimiter is ignored. Default is True.

lineterminatorstr, optional

String used to terminate lines produced by the writer. Default is a newline ("\n").

quotingint, optional

Quoting policy (one of the csv.QUOTE_* constants). Default is csv.QUOTE_MINIMAL.

Attributes:
dialectstr

Registered CSV dialect name.

logLog

Singleton logger instance used by the handler.

Methods

write_csv(file_or_path, data, headers=None)

Write data to a CSV file or an already-opened file object.

read_csv(filename=None, as_dict=False, content=None)

Read CSV data safely, returning an empty list on any error.

Notes

The dialect is registered with csv.register_dialect on every instantiation, replacing any dialect with the same name.

Examples

>>> handler = CSVHandler()  
>>> handler.read_csv(content="a;b\n1;2")  
[['a', 'b'], ['1', '2']]

read_csv

write_csv

Write a list of rows or dictionaries to CSV.
write_csv(file_or_path, data, headers=None)[source]

Write a list of rows or dictionaries to CSV.

Works with a file path or an already-opened file-like object (e.g. locked with portalocker).

Parameters:
file_or_pathstr | os.PathLike | TextIO

Destination file path or an open file object.

datalist[dict | list]

Rows to write. Dictionaries require headers.

headerslist[str] | None, optional

Field names when writing dictionaries. If provided, a header row is written first. Default is None.

Raises:
Exception

Any error while opening or writing is logged and re-raised.

Notes

With a path, parent directories are created if needed and the file is written in UTF-8 with BOM (utf-8-sig), so Excel detects the encoding. With an open file object, the caller is responsible for its mode, encoding and newline="".

read_csv(filename=None, as_dict=False, content=None)[source]

Read CSV data with comprehensive error handling.

Returns an empty list instead of raising exceptions for any problem (file missing, locked by Excel, wrong encoding, corrupted, etc.), so CSV issues never crash the application.

Parameters:
filenamestr | os.PathLike | None, optional

Path to the CSV file. Default is None.

as_dictbool, optional

If True, return a list of dictionaries using the first row as keys. Default is False.

contentstr | None, optional

CSV content provided directly as a string. Default is None.

Returns:
list[dict] | list[list[str]]

Rows as dictionaries if as_dict is True, otherwise as lists. Empty list on any read error.

Notes

If content is provided, filename is ignored; otherwise filename must be given.

A missing file is logged at INFO level (normal on the first run). Encodings are tried in order: utf-8-sig, the system’s preferred encoding (if not already listed), cp1252, utf-8 and latin1. A PermissionError (file locked, e.g. open in Excel) is logged as a warning; other read errors and a file that no encoding can decode are logged as errors.

Examples

>>> h = CSVHandler()  
>>> rows = "a;b\n1;2"
>>> h.read_csv(content=rows, as_dict=True)  
[{'a': '1', 'b': '2'}]
